title: Trump: What will happen to Trump’s tariffs after supreme court verdict?
description_short: Trump: What will happen to Trump’s tariffs after supreme court verdict?
description_medium: On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorize Trump’s challenged tariffs. Trump called the decision a “disgrace” and said he would keep tariffs in place under a different law. The ruling rejected that legal basis; it did not end every presidential tariff authority or settle refunds.
description_long: On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorize President Donald Trump to impose the challenged tariffs on imports. The decision affirmed lower-court findings that the tariffs imposed under that law were illegal. Trump called the ruling a “disgrace” and said he would continue his trade policy under other statutes. Hours after the decision, he announced a new 10% global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows tariffs of up to 15% for 150 days to address balance-of-payments problems. The Guardian explained that other tariff authorities have different limits and procedural requirements. The ruling also left open how importers might recover duties already paid; the process could involve Customs and Border Protection and lower courts. Trump dismissed immediate refunds and said litigation could continue for years. The decision struck down one legal basis for his tariff program, while the administration pursued another.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: What will happen to Trump’s tariffs after supreme court verdict?
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: What will happen to Trump’s tariffs after supreme court verdict?

notes: The Guardian reports the 6–3 IEEPA ruling, Trump’s response, the announced Section 122 tariff, and the unresolved refund process.

title: Trump named ‘undisputed champion of beautiful clean coal’ by industry group
description_short: Trump named ‘undisputed champion of beautiful clean coal’ by industry group
description_medium: At a White House ceremony on February 11, 2026, Donald Trump received a trophy naming him the “undisputed champion of beautiful clean coal.” The Guardian reported that the Washington Coal Club presented the award as Trump directed the Defense Department to buy billions of dollars’ worth of power from coal plants. Peabody Energy CEO James Grech presented the trophy.
description_long: Donald Trump received a “champion of beautiful clean coal” trophy during a White House ceremony on February 11, 2026. The Guardian reported that the award came from the Washington Coal Club, an advocacy group with financial ties to the coal industry, and that James Grech, chief executive of Peabody Energy, presented it. The ceremony coincided with Trump’s order directing the Defense Department to purchase billions of dollars’ worth of power from coal plants. The story links the industry group’s public recognition of Trump with a federal energy directive that could benefit coal producers. It does not establish that the award caused the order, identify the final procurement contracts, or specify how much electricity would be purchased from any individual plant. The documented event is the ceremony and the policy direction toward coal-generated power; the article does not report that the Pentagon had completed the purchases or quantify their eventual cost.

preserved_fields.title: Trump named ‘undisputed champion of beautiful clean coal’ by industry group
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump named ‘undisputed champion of beautiful clean coal’ by industry group

notes: The Guardian names the Washington Coal Club as the award-giving group and Peabody Energy CEO James Grech as presenter; it reports a directive to buy coal power, not completed purchases or contract terms.

title: El Salvador Prison Deportation - Erik Prince $100 Million Military Contractor Plan
description_short: El Salvador Prison Deportation - Erik Prince $100 Million Military Contractor Plan
description_medium: Politico reported on April 11, 2025, that Erik Prince pitched the administration a plan for a 10,000-person detention camp and deportations of up to 100,000 people to El Salvador. The report said White House interest was unclear. It described a contractor proposal, not an approved $100 million contract or an operating deportation program.
description_long: Donald Trump's administration negotiated with former Blackwater CEO Erik Prince to implement an 'unprecedented prison plan' that would deport '100,000 of the worst criminal offenders' to El Salvador prisons through a $100 million military contractor operation involving 10,000-person detention camps and private aircraft fleets operated by Prince's defense contracting network. The systematic foreign deportation represented Trump's implementation of the most extreme immigration enforcement proposal in American history, using military contractors to transport detained immigrants from U.S. prisons to foreign detention facilities while Prince's company handled logistics for gathering prisoners, processing immigration files, and operating international detention operations. The El Salvador prison plan violated international law and constitutional due process protections by sending U.S. residents to foreign prisons without judicial review, while creating unprecedented privatization of immigration enforcement through military contractors who had previously operated in war zones using violence and weapons against civilian populations. Prince's deportation proposal demonstrated Trump's willingness to outsource core government functions to private military contractors while creating profit opportunities for defense industry allies who saw 'potential profits in mass deportations' through government contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The foreign prison deportation violated sovereignty principles and international human rights law by using military contractors to forcibly transfer detainees to foreign countries without legal protections, judicial oversight, or diplomatic agreements ensuring humane treatment and legal representation for transported individuals. The unprecedented privatization represented what immigration advocates called 'extraordinary militarization' of deportation policy that treated immigration enforcement as military operation requiring private contractors with combat experience rather than law enforcement professionals trained in civil rights protections and due process procedures.
subcategory: Foreign Prison Deportation Through Military Contractors

title: Trump: ‘A subversion of the justice system’: DoJ shifts into Trump’s ‘political wing’ as criminal investigations accelerate
description_short: Trump: ‘A subversion of the justice system’: DoJ shifts into Trump’s ‘political wing’ as criminal investigations accelerate
description_medium: The Guardian reported on March 5, 2026, that former prosecutors saw politicization in the Justice Department under Attorney General Pam Bondi. Its examples included cases against James Comey and Letitia James that courts rejected, a grand jury’s refusal to indict Senator Mark Kelly and five other Democrats, and a Georgia election-office search tied to Trump’s 2020 fraud claims. The article attributes its broadest judgments to critics.
description_long: The Guardian’s March 5 report quoted former prosecutors who said the Justice Department under Attorney General Pam Bondi was being used to pursue Trump’s political and economic opponents. It pointed to charges against former FBI director James Comey and New York attorney general Letitia James that courts rejected as flawed. A grand jury on February 11 also declined to indict Senator Mark Kelly and five other Democrats over a video saying military members should refuse illegal orders; Trump had called their message “seditious behavior punishable by death.” The article further described an FBI search of a Georgia election office seeking evidence related to Trump’s debunked claim that he lost the 2020 election because of fraud. It noted that a banner bearing Trump’s image was displayed at Justice Department headquarters on February 19. The Guardian presented these events as evidence for the former prosecutors’ criticism of politicization. The reported cases and failed indictments are concrete events, while “subversion” and “political wing” are attributed assessments, not court findings. The report does not establish that every investigation was politically directed.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: ‘A subversion of the justice system’: DoJ shifts into Trump’s ‘political wing’ as criminal investigations accelerate
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: ‘A subversion of the justice system’: DoJ shifts into Trump’s ‘political wing’ as criminal investigations accelerate

notes: The Guardian article supplies examples of prosecutions, a declined grand-jury indictment, a Georgia election-office search, and expert criticism. The broad claims are attributed to former prosecutors, not presented as court findings.
